sections.h2: Weld County and its tax base
sections.html:
Weld County stretches across 4,017 square miles north of Denver, with Greeley as its seat. The 2020 census counted 328,981 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 378,426. Farmland, oil and gas, and fast-growing suburbs all feed the tax roll, which is why the Board of Equalization sets one appeal deadline for real property and the same deadline for personal property, oil and gas, and producing mines.

Cities such as Greeley, Evans, Fort Lupton and Dacono sit in the county, along with towns such as Windsor, Johnstown, Firestone, Frederick, Mead and Severance. Windsor, Johnstown and Erie cross into neighboring counties, so a house in one of them may be billed by Weld or by the other county.

sections.h2: Which Weld County offices handle property tax
sections.html:
Three offices share the work. The Assessor values property and prepares the tax roll, the Board of Equalization hears value appeals, and the Treasurer bills and collects. The Treasurer and Public Trustee office and the Assessor both work from 1400 N 17th Avenue in Greeley.

  • Assessor: assessor@weld.gov, (970) 353-3845.
  • County Board of Equalization: weld-cboe@weld.gov, (970) 400-3650. It hears appeals after the Notice of Determination.
  • Treasurer: PO Box 458, Greeley, CO 80632-0458, (970) 400-3290. It mails notices, collects tax and runs the lien sale.
  • Clerk and Recorder: 1250 H Street, Greeley, (970) 304-6530. It records the deed that changes the owner of record.

Notices from the Treasurer go out before the end of January to the owner of record on the roll the Assessor prepares.

Weld County taxes fall due January 1 for the previous year, so each bill covers the year before it arrives. The county posts three payment dates: February 28 for the first half, June 15 for the second half and April 30 for full payment.

Half payments must be equal installments, and partial payments are refused. When the tax is $25.00 or less, the half-payment option is off the table and the whole amount is due on the full payment date. A payment with a U.S. postmark on or before the deadline is on time.

That is the delinquent interest chart on the Treasurer's tax information page. Dates are reset every year, so check the page for the current ones.

The Treasurer takes payment by mail, online, in person or through a drop box.

  • Mail: send a check, money order or cashier's check payable to Weld County Treasurer to PO Box 458, Greeley, CO 80632-0458, with the payment coupon for each property.
  • Online: weldtax.com takes electronic checks for free, while debit or credit cards carry a third-party fee.
  • In person: 1400 N 17th Avenue, Greeley, where cash, checks, money orders, cashier's checks and cards are all accepted. A Visa debit card costs a flat $4.00.
  • Drop box: checks only, north of the main building entrance. Cash and lien payments do not go in the box.

If you and your mortgage company both pay, the Treasurer processes the mortgage company's payment and returns yours. The mortgage company gets no copy of your notice from the county, so an escrow customer who wants the lender to have one should send a photocopy.

Start with a protest to the Assessor. If you still disagree, appeal to the County Board of Equalization. The Board of Commissioners acts as that Board under C.R.S. 39-8-101, and it can review only the property's value, not the amount of tax charged.

The value on a 2025 or 2026 bill is the Assessor's estimate as of June 30, 2024, a date set by law. For those years the Board considers only sales and market information from 2023 and the first six months of 2024, so a purchase or appraisal after June 30, 2024 cannot be used.

The Board of Equalization sets one deadline for real property and for personal property, oil and gas, and producing mines. It was September 15, counted by received or postmarked date, in the 2026 cycle, and the Board of Equalization page posts each year's date. Appeals must be in writing. File online, by mail, in person, by fax at (970) 304-6433 or by email. Phone appeals are not accepted.

Only the owner has standing. Someone filing for the owner needs a signed letter of agency. Late appeals are not considered.

sections.h2: What happens to the tax bill when you sell
sections.html:
Tax follows the parcel, so an unpaid bill is settled at or before closing, usually by the title company. Colorado taxes are paid in arrears, which generally leaves the seller owing tax for the part of the year they owned the house. The title company works out the split on the settlement statement.

To confirm the amount owed, title companies use the Treasurer's Certificate of Taxes Due request form. If there are back taxes, request it early, because the interest chart above keeps climbing every month.

After the sale, the new owner's name reaches the tax roll only through the recorded deed. The Assessor updates the name once the deed is recorded with the Clerk and Recorder. A bill that never arrives does not excuse nonpayment under C.R.S. 39-10-103.

sections.h2: If Weld County taxes go unpaid
sections.html:
Interest is added each month a payment is late. Lien payments must be made at the Treasurer's office and processed by the last business day of the month, because postmarks and drop box items do not count for liens.

For an owner who is behind, timing is the main issue. Interest builds monthly, and a sale lets the title company pay the arrears from the proceeds. We buy Weld County houses as is, so if you want to talk through a house with back taxes, we can answer with a written offer. Gather your most recent notice and the Treasurer's payoff figure first, and the conversation will be quicker.

The Treasurer's tax page has sections on senior programs, tax deferral and special assessments, and the Board of Equalization page links to Senior Property Tax Exemptions. Read them before you list, because a deferral or exemption in place on your account may change what the title company has to settle.

sections.h2: Steps for a seller with a Weld County bill
sections.html: Order matters when you sell. First, find your most recent notice and see which installments are paid. Second, ask the title company to request the Certificate of Taxes Due. Third, confirm that the mailing address is current, since the county sends the notice to the owner of record. Fourth, if you have a mortgage, ask the servicer whether it pays your tax from escrow. Last, after closing, make sure the deed is recorded so the new owner's name reaches the roll. These steps take little time, and they prevent most tax surprises at the settlement table.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Weld County, Colorado?
faqs.a: Taxes are due January 1 for the previous year. The county lists February 28 for the first half, June 15 for the second half and April 30 for full payment.

faqs.q: What is the Weld County property tax appeal deadline?
faqs.a: The Board of Equalization's deadline for real property appeals was September 15 in 2026, received or postmarked, and it posts the date each year. Late appeals are not considered.

faqs.q: Can I pay half of my Weld County property tax?
faqs.a: Yes, in two equal installments, unless the tax is $25.00 or less. The county does not accept partial payments.

faqs.q: Do I get a Weld County tax notice if my mortgage company pays my taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The Treasurer mails the notice to the owner of record, and mortgage companies do not receive a copy from the county.

faqs.q: How do I get a Certificate of Taxes Due in Weld County?
faqs.a: Use the request form on the Treasurer's tax information page. Title companies commonly request it before closing.
